batchName: Empire: Claudius and Nero (AD 41-68) - Latin words
description: Written by hand from the chapter text: the Latin words it explains

questions.question: What were the liberti who ran Claudius’s offices?
questions.explanation: They headed offices for letters, finance and justice, and senators were appalled.
questions.sourceQuote: he relied on freedmen (*liberti*), former slaves

questions.question: What was the Domus Aurea that Nero built after the fire?
options: The Golden House, his new palace
questions.explanation: It had landscaped parks and a statue of Nero about 30 m tall.

questions.question: Camulodunum became a colonia. What was that?
options: A market town of the Britons
questions.explanation: It was the capital of the new province, with a great temple to Claudius.
questions.sourceQuote: Camulodunum, modern Colchester, became a colony (*colonia*), a settlement of retired soldiers

questions.question: What did the quinquennium Neronis mean?
questions.explanation: His tutor and the commander of the guard steered government in those years.

questions.question: In AD 47 Claudius revived the office of censor. What did a censor do?
options: Kept the lists of citizens and senators
questions.explanation: He used it to admit nobles from Gaul into the Senate.
questions.sourceQuote: he revived the old office of censor (*censor*), who kept the lists of citizens and senators.

questions.question: In AD 68 the Senate declared Nero hostis publicus. What did it mean?
questions.explanation: He fled and took his own life on 9 June AD 68.
questions.sourceQuote: The Senate declared Nero a public enemy (*hostis publicus*).

questions.question: Claudius sent four legiones to Britain. What was a legio?
options: A heavy infantry division of several thousand men
questions.explanation: Four legions crossed the Channel in AD 43.
questions.sourceQuote: Claudius sent four legions (*legiones*), Rome's heavy infantry divisions of several thousand men each

questions.question: After Nero’s death, many portraits were defaced as part of damnatio memoriae. What was it?
options: The condemnation of a ruler’s memory
questions.explanation: Yet people went on making images of him.
questions.sourceQuote: the condemnation of a ruler's memory (*damnatio memoriae*)
